newsitem.title: USA: Fate of 39 state tobacco suits unresolved by pact.
newsitem.headline: Fate of 39 state tobacco suits unresolved by pact.

text.p: The tobacco industry's settlement of what would have been the first trial of a state Medicaid suit against cigarette makers leaves unresolved the fate of 39 other cases across the country.

On Thursday Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore and the nation's four largest cigarette makers announced they had reached an agreement in which the companies would pay the state more than $3 billion over 25 years.

But the pact does not necessarily mean that the industry will reach similar agreements with other states. A total of 40 state attorneys general, including Mississippi, sued the industry to recoup the Medicaid costs of sick smokers.

Indeed, both the tobacco industry and a number of attorneys general said Thursday's agreement underscores the need for a national settlement of litigation. Last month the groups proposed a broad $368.5 billion settlement that is now pending before Congress and the White House.

"Neither this (Mississippi settlement) nor any one state can achieve the sweeping public health benefits now before Congress," said Connecticut Attorney General Richard Blumenthal, who helped negotiate last month's historic accord.

"The settlement resolves certain legal and financial issues in one state, but it does not -- and could not -- address broader issues of concern in Mississippi and throughout the nation," the tobacco companies said.
The landmark national pact, which includes health care concessions from cigarette makers, has been criticized as too lenient by a number of members of Congress who must approve it.
There is particular concern about funding and language which critics believe will present the Food and Drug Administration with unnecessary regulatory hurdles in its efforts to control cigarettes.
President Clinton has said the tobacco settlement must not be allowed to paralyze the FDA.

With the agreement's fate uncertain, the states must settle their lawsuits individually or go to trial. Many are hoping that Congress will pass legislation settling litigation before they must take their cases to court.
"I don't think settling this (Mississippi) case necessarily means that others will be settled," Blumenthal said.

He said that while the terms also may not set a precedent in other negotiations, he was hopeful the pact signaled that the industry was willing to treat other states fairly and that many might receive more than being sought in their suits.
Meanwhile, Florida Attorney General Bob Butterworth, whose case is scheduled for trial on Aug. 4, said Thursday that no deal was imminent to settle the state's $1 billion Medicaid suit.
He said he last met tobacco negotiators on June 26 and did not expect to bargain again for at least another two weeks.

"We're four weeks away from jury selection. It'll be another month before a judge will hear opening statements .... Given the fact our case is at least a couple months away, I think it would be a little premature for both sides to discuss settlement in the Florida case," he said.

In Texas, where the state's Medicaid trial is scheduled to begin Sept. 29, a spokeswoman for the attorneys general office said no negotiations are being held now with the tobacco industry. She said the state is preparing for trial.
Minnesota Attorney General Hubert Humphrey, who has opposed the terms of the national settlement, vowed to keep fighting his suit.

"The Mississippi settlement is an acknowledgment that aggressive pursuit of the states' lawsuits is the best path to justice," he said. "The over $3 billion settlement sets a minimum floor for those states with antitrust, consumer fraud, and treble damages claims that were not even alleged in the Mississippi case."
